blocks.content: The High Court is the highest judicial authority at the state level in India. It functions under Part VI, Chapter V of the Constitution of India. The provisions regarding High Courts are mainly contained in Articles 214–231.
1. Constitutional Articles Related to High Courts

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: High Courts are established under Article 214, with Article 231 allowing Parliament to create a common High Court for two or more states.
High Court judges are appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
To be eligible for appointment, a candidate must be a citizen of India with 10 years of judicial office experience or 10 years as an advocate in a High Court.
A High Court judge holds office until attaining the age of 62 years and can be removed by the President following an address by Parliament.
High Courts possess original, appellate, supervisory, and writ jurisdictions under Article 226, making them Courts of Record with Judicial Review powers.

blocks.content: 2. Composition of High Court
• A High Court consists of a Chief Justice and other judges.
• The number of judges is decided by the President depending on workload.
3. Appointment of High Court Judges
• Judges are appointed by the President of India.

The writ jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 is wider than that of the Supreme Court under Article 32 because the High Court can issue writs not only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights but also for any other legal right.
• Consultation with Chief Justice of India, Governor, and Chief Justice of High Court.
4. Qualifications of High Court Judges
• Citizen of India.
• 10 years judicial office OR 10 years advocate in High Court.
5. Tenure

blocks.content: • Judges retire at age 62.
• They can resign to the President.
• They can be removed through impeachment.
6. Jurisdiction of High Court
Original, Appellate, Writ, and Supervisory jurisdiction.
7. Types of Writs

items: Article 226 writ jurisdiction is wider than Article 32 because High Courts can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.
The 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963 raised the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62 years.
Calcutta High Court, established in 1862, is the oldest High Court in India.
Parliament holds the power to extend or exclude the jurisdiction of a High Court over any Union Territory.

blocks.content: EXAM Important Facts
• Articles 214–231 deal with High Courts.
• Judges retire at 62.
• High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
